title: When Should We Intervene at Test Time?

paper.title: When Should We Intervene at Test Time?
paper.abstract: Abstract Test-time adaptation helps a deployed model respond to changing inputs, but the same intervention can rescue one batch and damage the next. Updating normalization statistics, for example, can improve corrupted images yet fail when a batch contains mostly one class. Average accuracy hides these failures and cannot tell a model when to use an intervention. Target labels can guide this decision, but they are scarce and some choices are already clear. We introduce PORTAL, a controller that chooses when to deploy an intervention, which inputs to label, and when to stop querying. Each available prediction rule is a candidate, and its predictions are fixed before current feedback arrives. Every acquired label therefore evaluates all candidates on the same input. PORTAL combines these shared comparisons and directs queries toward candidates that can still overtake the current leader. It stops when the remaining labels cannot change the choice or when the possible accuracy gain no longer justifies another query. Our analysis links the required feedback to accuracy gaps and shared mistakes, explaining why some choices need much less evidence. Experiments show that this control turns an intervention that loses accuracy overall into a useful choice on selected batches. It prevents severe failures caused by changes in arrival order and preserves gains across complete corruption streams. When a fixed rule already works well, PORTAL uses little feedback to retain its performance. Periodic label checks reveal when past evidence needs refreshing and help the controller recover as conditions change. The acquired labels also train stronger candidates for future batches, and selection brings nearly all of their accuracy gains into deployment. The same feedback therefore improves both the choice made now and the predictions available to later batches.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: A deployed model encounters changes in both image appearance and class composition. Fog may replace clear weather, or one object class may dominate a run of inputs. Test-time adaptation responds by changing the model as data arrive. Yet an update that rescues one batch can break predictions on the next. Its average gain across a test set does not tell us when to use it. Consider batch normalization (BN), which normalizes activations using feature statistics. Recomputing these statistics on incoming images often helps under corruption. Averaging predictions from an image and its horizontally flipped view offers another intervention. We call each available prediction rule a candidate . Existing adaptation methods provide many such candidates ( Wang et al., 2021 ; Niu et al., 2022 ; Niu et al., 2023 ) . A fixed rule chooses one for the whole stream. Local selection chooses for each batch, retaining the unchanged model when an intervention is unhelpful. The need for selection becomes clear on PACS, which contains Photo, Art, Cartoon and Sketch domains. Combining BN updates with original and flipped views gives BN+flip. This candidate works well when domains arrive in blocks or are mixed together. Grouping inputs by class, called class-block arrivals , changes the batch statistics and reduces its accuracy to 22.58%. We introduce Portal , a controller that uses sparse target labels to choose among the available predictions. 1 1 1 Code, data, and manuscript: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/PORTAL-8322/ . It reaches 51.28% under the same arrivals. Choosing well requires evidence, but labels are scarce. Active test-time adaptation acquires labels to guide updates and selection ( Gui et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Wang and Ding, 2025 ) ; adaptive labeling also supports evaluation under shift ( Mittal et al., 2024 ) . A close comparison may cost more feedback than its accuracy gain is worth. The controller must decide which candidate to deploy, which input to label, and when to stop. Appendix X places these decisions in the broader literature. Portal uses one label to evaluate every candidate on the same input. Agreement gives candidates the same outcome; disagreement reveals which predictions are correct. We group inputs by the classes that candidates predict and estimate class probabilities within each group. Every label updates all comparisons, including the overlap between errors. Queries target rivals that can overtake the leader within the remaining budget. Selection stops when no remaining labels can change the winner or when the possible accuracy gain cannot justify another query. Our analysis relates the feedback requirement to accuracy gaps and shared errors. It also shows why biased queries can make a wrong choice more certain. Earlier labels reduce query costs while their class relationships remain stable; periodic checks reveal when comparisons need refreshing. After choosing among fixed predictions, we use the new labels to train stronger candidates for later batches. Our experiments follow this progression from intervention failure to future learning. Holding a candidate fixed shows that targeted feedback turns its aggregate accuracy loss into a gain. A more harmful transfer shows how selection prevents most of an intervention’s damage. Complete ImageNet-C corruption streams test control at scale. CIFAR comparisons show the label savings when a strong fixed rule already works well. Finally, learned candidates raise PACS deployment accuracy from 59.68% to 72.64%. The same labels improve current deployment decisions and train stronger candidates for later batches.

sections.heading: Learning after selection.
sections.text: A label can help beyond the current decision. After comparing the fixed predictions, we use it to train the next batch’s classifier. Uniform queries fill any unused training allowance, and each label is counted once. Paired experiments retain or undo an update to measure its effect on later predictions (Appendix F ).

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: We first expose intervention failures, then hold the candidates fixed to measure the effect of control. Full corruption streams test the scale of the effect. We next examine stopping and changing evidence, before using the same feedback to train stronger candidates. Accuracy differences are in percentage points (pp). The main comparisons use ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10-C/100-C and a Photo-trained ResNet-50 on PACS. ImageNet-C uses a ResNet-50 updated by EATTA, an active test-time adaptation method ( Wang and Ding, 2025 ) . Natural-domain tests use contrastive language–image pretraining (CLIP), with a large vision transformer and 14-pixel patches (ViT-L/14). Its readout maps features to class scores. CIFAR-10.1 supplies newly collected images ( Recht et al., 2018 ) . Fixed rules use the unchanged model, BN, horizontal flip, or BN+flip. We also compare their mean-logit ensemble. Empirical risk minimization (ERM) selects the candidate with the fewest queried errors, using a fixed tie rule. Its queries are uniform, prioritize class disagreements, or target symmetric KL divergence between prediction probabilities (Top-KL). Shared-feedback comparisons keep query and evaluation inputs separate. Historical paired-admission tests use queried-error comparisons. Their protocols are described below; the shared-posterior experiments use Section 2 .

sections.heading: 4.1 Arrival order can break a strong intervention
sections.text: On PACS, BN+flip works well when domains arrive in blocks or are mixed together. Grouping images by class changes its behavior sharply. Accuracy falls to 22.58%, below the unchanged model’s 50.88%. Portal chooses among the same predictions and reaches 51.28%. Local selection prevents the fixed intervention from turning a change in arrival order into a large accuracy loss. Figure 2 also measures net batch harm : positive batch error increases over the unchanged model, summed and divided by evaluation size. New errors count previously correct predictions made wrong. These measures distinguish the damage an intervention causes from its net accuracy. 22.58 51.28 Figure 2: A strong fixed intervention fails when classes arrive together. On class-block PACS, BN+flip reaches 22.58% accuracy and Portal reaches 51.28%. Net batch harm falls from 32.41 to 0.34 percentage points. Domain, Mixed and Class denote domain blocks, mixed domains and class blocks. Results use a Photo source and batch size 64. Bars average three orders; accuracy error bars show order standard deviation (SD). The inset enlarges the selectors’ harm values.

sections.heading: Adding candidates can help or hurt.
sections.text: A separate controlled experiment expands the candidate set, or portfolio . Expansion raises error by 14.32 points under a HILTTA-style controller ( Li et al., 2024 ) . Under Portal , it lowers error by 1.24 points. This yields a 15.56-point controller–portfolio interaction across ten seeds (Appendix R ). We next fix the predictions to measure the effect of control directly.

sections.text: We use paired admission : deploy a challenger only when it makes fewer queried errors than the incumbent. Ties keep the incumbent. The historical PACS replay holds the incumbent, horizontal-view challenger and 816 batches fixed. Its Portal rule targets three symmetric-KL queries per batch; admission then equals ERM on those labels. sections.heading: Control on a full corruption stream.
sections.text: In a shared-prefix variant, EATTA reuses the sequence of selection labels for its committed update. On 750,000 ImageNet-C images, error falls from 50.14% to 49.55%, improving all 15 corruptions. Of admitted batches, 77.3% benefit. Accepted choices stop after a mean prefix of 2.87 labels. Across all batches, the mean prefix is 3.999 labels. Trial updates access additional labels outside this count (Appendix J ). With separate acquisition, three selection labels in addition to three adaptation labels reduce error by 1.008 points. This retains 73.37% of the fixed challenger’s gain. An independent full stream gives 0.982 points. Appendix J reports both protocols and six benchmarks’ fixed-intervention and readout comparisons.

sections.heading: 4.4 Small label budgets can resolve real advantages
sections.text: Figure 4: Exact selection-error probabilities for brightness (left) and JPEG (right). Curves use uniform sampling without replacement; markers use 2,000 independent subset draws per setting. Means cover three checkpoints. Schedules use distinct image blocks. We compare BN+flip and mean logits on streams with disjoint image sets per corruption segment. BN+flip wins on noise; mean logits wins on brightness and JPEG. We sample uniformly from each segment’s full query pool. Selection favors fewer queried errors, with BN+flip breaking ties (Appendix W.5 ). Even 75 labels leave a 24–39% probability of choosing the worse output (Figure 4 ). Exact probabilities agree with independent subset draws. Knowing that a better candidate exists does not make it easy to identify.

sections.heading: 4.8 Retaining an update changes future predictions
sections.text: A useful current choice need not improve the next batch. We compare two model copies with identical future inputs, labels and updates. One retains the current update; the other undoes it. Retaining the update gains 0.23 points now but changes next-batch accuracy by − 0.20 -0.20 points. Undoing it leaves future predictions unchanged. Appendix F relates these effects to the update dynamics and bounds the later loss change. Learning a candidate and deciding when to deploy it remain distinct decisions.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: An intervention’s value depends on the batch it receives. A rule that helps under ordinary arrivals can fail when classes arrive together. Portal uses shared feedback to choose when to deploy each candidate and stops buying labels when they cannot improve that choice. Holding the challenger fixed shows how targeted feedback turns an aggregate loss into useful local gains. Periodic checks keep the evidence current. The same labels train stronger future candidates, and selection brings their gains to deployment.

sections.heading: Reproducibility statement
sections.text: The appendix contains the model settings, query/evaluation splits, update timing, query budgets, and statistical procedures. It also provides complete corruption and domain results, comparisons of method components, and proofs. The changing-label experiments include their selector definitions, reconstructed comparison methods, and independent sampling units. The manuscript, implementation, released result data, and available frozen prediction banks are provided in our anonymous repository: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/PORTAL-8322/ . Its data inventory lists the external datasets and checkpoints needed for further reproduction.

sections.heading: F.7 Update timing and experimental verification
sections.text: At a chosen batch t t , we score an intervention and either retain or undo its update. We call this the branch point. sections.heading: Appendix G Experimental populations, feedback and outputs
sections.text: The experiments measure fixed intervention capacity, its realization through output selection, and its expansion through learned states. Each comparison retains its model, evaluation population, output timing and annotation budget.

sections.heading: Corruption populations.
sections.text: CIFAR10-C and CIFAR100-C use all 15 severity-5 corruptions and three source ResNet18 checkpoints. Each corruption contains 10,000 images. Batches contain 64 images, including a final batch of 16. The total is 150,000 images per dataset and checkpoint. A permanent split assigns 5,000 base-image indices to the query population Q Q and 5,000 to the evaluation population E E . The role of an underlying image is unchanged across corruptions and checkpoints. Each corruption is a separate deployment: selection statistics and annotation history reset at its boundary. An annotation purchased in one deployment is charged again if queried in another.

sections.heading: Natural domain shifts.
sections.text: The CLIP ViT-L/14 experiments include all four domains of PACS, OfficeHome and VLCS, with 9,991, 15,588 and 7,510 image instances, respectively. Their permanent query/evaluation counts are 5,070/4,921, 7,801/7,787 and 3,751/3,759. The split is assigned to encoded-content groups, so repeated occurrences remain on the same side. All dataset instances and their original annotations are retained. OfficeHome has 15,176 content groups, including 87 groups whose 178 occurrences have conflicting directory labels. VLCS contains 7,506 groups and no conflicting labels. PACS has no repeated content in this enumeration. Annotation costs count queried instances. PACS and VLCS identities are recorded during inference. OfficeHome identities follow the deterministic class/file order of its saved four-readout stream and are checked against its stored labels.

sections.heading: Timing and aggregation.
sections.text: Fixed whole-dataset scores include every example and use zero target labels. Controlled comparisons score the common E E population after acquiring current-batch labels from Q Q . These labels choose among predictions already formed. In the online-classifier experiment, they train the classifier after current predictions have been scored. That update affects later batches. CIFAR scores pool equal-size corruption populations. Vision-language model (VLM) results report both equal-domain and image-pooled accuracy, with the equal-domain mean as primary. Standard deviations cover three CIFAR checkpoints or five natural-domain stream orders, as indicated in each table.

sections.heading: Query rules and defaults.
sections.text: Empirical selection minimizes queried classification errors and keeps the designated default on ties. Uniform querying samples three available Q Q examples. Disagreement-first querying prioritizes inputs with different candidate class predictions, in random order. Symmetric-KL querying ranks disagreement between predicted class probabilities. The complete CIFAR experiment sums the six pairwise scores; the four-readout CLIP experiment uses their mean. Both give the same ranking for a fixed candidate set. The StatA and convex-readout experiments use the largest pairwise score. The fixed default is BN+flip on CIFAR and the eight-view readout on CLIP. Portal uses total prior mass 1: it assigns 0.75 to candidate-predicted classes and spreads the remaining 0.25 over all classes (Equation ( 86 )). The label price is 0.002, with at most 12 queries per batch. Three query credits arrive per batch. CIFAR caps the stored balance at 12; the VLM experiments carry all unused credits. Tables report actual label use.

sections.heading: Appendix Q Dynamic conditions, source changes and class-label noise
sections.text: Batch composition changes normalization-based predictions. We regenerate all four ResNet outputs for each condition and keep every target image once per stream. Three arrival orders are tested with four source checkpoints. For the Photo source, batch sizes are 16,32,64,128. At batch size 64, we test mixed, reversed, gradually overlapping, and class-block orders. Art, Cartoon, and Sketch source models are each evaluated on the remaining three domains. This gives 33 complete runs. The original query/evaluation roles remain fixed. Photo images, used as targets for the other source models, receive a content-based split before evaluation.

sections.heading: Arrival construction.
sections.text: Domain-block streams shuffle images within each domain. Reverse streams reverse the domain order while preserving their within-domain permutations. Mixed streams uniformly permute all target images. For gradual transitions, the within-domain normalized rank receives Gaussian jitter of standard deviation 0.45 0.45 before sorting across domains; overlapping regions retain every image once. Class-block streams group the benchmark’s labels within each domain, constructing temporally imbalanced arrivals. sections.heading: Budget handling.
sections.text: The fixed-prediction PACS and VLM experiments accrue three labels per batch, carry unspent credits, and permit at most twelve acquisitions within a batch. The complete CIFAR frozen-selection experiment caps the stored balance at twelve as well as the within-batch count. Fixed-three baselines acquire three eligible labels, including on agreement inputs when needed. Their budget is reduced only when the eligible pool has fewer than three examples. The learned-readout experiments use three total labels in each batch: the selector can spend part of this budget on output evidence and uniform sampling supplies the remainder for the subsequent learned state. That total includes all labels used for either purpose.

sections.heading: Computational structure.
sections.text: Posterior means require O ⁡ ( S ​ K ) O(SK) operations and the full covariance O ⁡ ( S ​ K 2 ) O(SK^{2}) . The finite-horizon reachability calculation processes at most S ​ K ​ B SKB marginal increments for local allowance B B , with sorting in the current implementation. One-label value evaluates C C possible outcomes per eligible stratum and competitive action. The matrices have candidate dimension, independent of the feature encoder’s parameter count. sections.heading: S.4 Convex-readout implementation
sections.text: Section P defines the supervised simplex objective, its Hessian and target-Fisher query score. The implementation centers every candidate’s class logits, initializes the weights uniformly, and solves the strictly convex objective with analytic-gradient SLSQP at tolerance 10 − 9 10^{-9} . The comparison uses the same queried examples for each fitted mixture and its discrete ERM control. Uniform, disagreement and maximum-pair-KL acquisition use their declared score, while target Fisher recomputes Equation ( 85 ) after every label. Evaluation inputs contribute unlabeled logits to the target curvature and supply labels only to the scorer. Tables 46 – 48 contain every regularizer, acquisition, output rule and probability metric.

sections.heading: V.1 Contextual active model selection with permanent query roles
sections.text: Contextual Active Model Selection (CAMS) ( Liu et al., 2024 ) chooses a model for each input. We apply its stochastic procedure to the four fixed PACS candidates: identity, BN, flip, and BN+flip. Each of four advice policies recommends one candidate. CAMS combines these policies through exponential weights and smoothed advice, then samples a model. It chooses that model before deciding whether to request the label. Label requests follow an entropy-dependent Bernoulli probability, and policy losses use inverse-probability weights. Only permanent query inputs can be labeled. CAMS restarts at domain boundaries. The cumulative caps 131,393,655 are allocated to domains in proportion to their batch counts, corresponding to nominal budgets one,three,five. The algorithm can stop below its cap because its native requests remain stochastic. Five stream orders couple their own selector randomization to the fixed prediction banks. BN predictions are generated from the full unlabeled batch, so the per-example action timing applies to model selection while feature computation remains batch based. With four single-candidate advice policies, CAMS smoothing assigns 7 / 16 7/16 probability to the recommended model and 3 / 16 3/16 to each other model. Model choice remains random even when one policy dominates. Our implementation retains this distribution. sections.heading: Appendix X Related work
sections.text: The literature offers many ways to change a deployed model. It also offers ways to judge whether a change helps. Portal brings these two questions together through a shared label budget.

sections.heading: X.1 Feedback and the risk of a wrong choice
sections.text: Adaptive labeling and label-free accuracy estimation help evaluate models after distribution shift ( Mittal et al., 2024 ; Lee et al., 2024c ) . Accuracy–agreement relations provide another signal from unlabeled data ( Kim et al., 2024 ) . Binary feedback reduces the amount of information requested from an annotator ( Lee et al., 2025a ) . In our setting, a full class label judges every candidate on the same input. Feedback can lose its value as the stream changes. Risk monitoring, protected entropy matching, and domain-shift detection track different signs of trouble ( Schirmer et al., 2025 ; Bar et al., 2024 ; Park et al., 2025a ) . Recovery time and prediction latency add two costs beyond current accuracy ( Zhou et al., 2026 ; Sreeram et al., 2026 ) . Our drift experiments measure how quickly fresh labels can replace stale evidence in the selection decision. The deployment population may also change in ways that a prediction pattern hides. Open-set inputs, malicious test samples, and noisy inputs challenge adaptation in different ways ( Gao et al., 2024 ; Park et al., 2024 ; Cao et al., 2025 ) . Domain compensation addresses open-set streams, while selective adaptation isolates a shifted modality ( Yang et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) . Long-tailed classes add another source of unequal feedback ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . These settings make the link between queried and deployed inputs a substantive part of the decision.

sections.heading: X.2 How candidate predictions change
sections.text: An intervention can update a model through self-training or prediction energy ( Ma, 2024 ; Yuan et al., 2024 ) . Disentangled objectives show that prediction entropy alone does not describe every useful update ( Lee et al., 2024b ) . Ranked entropy and entropy–energy duality refine the signal used for adaptation ( Han et al., 2025 ; Park et al., 2025b ) . Uncertainty calibration, Tsallis entropy, and sharpness-aware regularization offer further choices ( Tan et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2026b ; Niu et al., 2025 ) . Bayesian updates and online expectation–maximization change how a candidate uses incoming examples ( Zhou et al., 2025 ; Dai and Yang, 2025 ) . Inter-class topology and adaptive representation alignment address structure across a changing stream ( Ni et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2024b ) . Each method creates predictions that can be judged against a fixed rule on the next deployment batch. An update’s state can live in batch-normalization memory, an organized example buffer, or a tracked subspace ( Kang et al., 2024 ; Zhu et al., 2024 ; Duan et al., 2025 ) . Expert blending chooses an input-dependent mixture ( Lee et al., 2024a ) . Diffusion-based transformations change corruptions or align an input with a synthetic domain ( Oh et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) . Our retain-versus-undo experiment measures the later effect of keeping one such state change. The cost of constructing a candidate also matters. Forward-only adaptation, backpropagation-free alignment, and activation-function adaptation alter the required computation ( Niu et al., 2024 ; Ma et al., 2026 ; Kim et al., 2026 ) . Sparse updates and activation sparsity reduce work or memory ( Cha et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2025 ) . Cloud–edge distillation, cross-device merging, and zeroth-order prompt optimization offer other deployment choices ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Mitsuzumi et al., 2026 ; Wang and Wang, 2026 ) . Label cost and computation cost remain distinct when choosing a complete system.

sections.heading: X.3 Vision–language prediction rules
sections.text: Simple adaptation rules and analyses of zero-shot generalization provide strong starting points for vision–language models ( Farina et al., 2024 ; Zanella and Ayed, 2024 ) . Regional bootstrapping, attribute prompts, and hierarchical knowledge change what the model sees or asks of a class ( Zhang et al., 2024a ; Zhang et al., 2025a ; Zhang et al., 2025b ) . Semantic integration and dynamic prompts offer further candidate rules ( Huang et al., 2025a ; Xiao et al., 2025 ) . A prompt coreset carries selected context across the stream ( Zhang et al., 2025c ) . Candidates can also use spatial bias, both modalities, or fewer visual tokens ( Huang et al., 2025b ; Maharana et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) . Retrieval and label propagation use neighboring examples to change predictions ( Lee et al., 2025b ; Fan et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025c ) . Prototypes and attributive–associative memory retain different summaries of past inputs ( Huang et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., ) . Dual debiasing and dynamic logit adjustment modify the final scores ( Luo et al., ; Wu et al., 2026a ) . These designs enlarge the set of rules that a selector may compare. Flatness-guided and robust prompt methods target prediction stability ( Li et al., 2025a ; Zhu et al., 2026 ; Kim and Um, 2026 ) . Flatness-aware pretraining addresses prompt calibration ( Jang et al., 2026 ) . Bilateral information use and universal prompt learning explore different sources of test-time signal ( Sun et al., 2026 ; Fu et al., 2026 ) . Test-time adaptation also supports zero-shot value functions ( Ziakas and Russo, 2026 ) . Beyond single-label classification, cross-modal retrieval and multi-label prediction need different outputs ( Li et al., 2025b ; Wu et al., 2025 ) . Our experiments use a shared class label so that one query directly compares all candidate rules.
